newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland sets up EU currency taskforce.
newsitem.headline: Ireland sets up EU currency taskforce.

text.p: Irish trade minister Enda Kenny said on Friday that he had set up an EU currency task force to help exporters experiencing difficulties because of the Irish pound's recent appreciation against certain European currencies.

The Irish pound has gained more than 11 percent against the mark in the last six months and is currently perched at the top of the ERM grid, more than 11 percent above the French franc, the weakest currency.
The taskforce will assess the impact of fluctuations in European exchange rates on Irish companies and help firms to obtain higher margins on their exports, Kenny said in a statement.
It will operate under the aegis of the Irish Trade Board and will be modelled on a sterling taskforce which assisted firms experiencing problems because of sterling fluctuations last year.
The sterling taskforce contacted over 450 companies with significant exports to the UK and found that only 10 percent experienced significant problems from sterling volatility.
A further 50 percent has been affected but were coping while 40 percent of companies said sterling was not an issue.

Kenny said exchange rate problems have always been and will continue to be a factor in international trade and Ireland remains very vulnerable to such fluctuations because it has such a small, open economy.

"This is a core reason why the government are so committed to becoming a founder member of EMU in order to stabilise our long-term economic growth and to minimise such problems in the future," he said.
Kenny also said the government's ability to influence external exchange rates in favour of particular sectors was extremely limited.

"The primary responsibility for dealing with currency fluctuations rests with firms themselves. In the short term, firms can guard against these by hedging and other devices but, in the long term, the only answer is to be as flexible and competitive as possible," he said.
Kenny also noted that exchange rate movements have a "swings and roundabouts" dimension.

In the years before 1995, the Irish pound depreciated significantly against the mark and other European currencies and the firms who are experiencing difficulties now enjoyed very favourable trading conditions in those years, he said.
